{
"Distributed System": "A collection of independent computing nodes that coordinate over a network to appear and function as a single coherent system to end users. These systems must address challenges such as concurrency, partial failures, and lack of a global clock.",
"Network Latency": "The time delay incurred when transmitting data between nodes across a network, affecting the responsiveness and coordination of distributed components. It is a fundamental constraint that distributed systems must account for in their design.",
"Failure": "An event in which a component of a distributed system, such as a node, process, or network link, ceases to function correctly or becomes unreachable. Failures may be partial, transient, or permanent and must be anticipated by resilient system designs.",
"Asynchrony": "A property of distributed systems in which there are no guaranteed bounds on message delivery times or process execution speeds. Asynchrony complicates coordination and detection of failures among nodes.",
"Consensus Algorithm": "A protocol that enables a group of distributed nodes to agree on a single value or sequence of operations despite failures and asynchrony. It is foundational for maintaining consistent state across replicas.",
"Raft": "A consensus algorithm designed for understandability that elects a leader to manage log replication and ensures agreement on state among a cluster of nodes. It provides strong consistency guarantees while tolerating node failures.",
"State Agreement": "The property by which multiple nodes in a distributed system converge on a shared, consistent view of system state. It is typically achieved through consensus or coordination protocols.",
"Replication": "The practice of maintaining copies of data or services on multiple nodes to improve availability, durability, and fault tolerance. Replication requires mechanisms to keep replicas synchronized or consistent.",
"Availability": "The degree to which a system remains operational and able to service requests, often measured as a percentage of uptime. High availability is typically achieved through redundancy and replication.",
"Fault Tolerance": "The ability of a distributed system to continue functioning correctly despite the failure of some of its components. It is achieved through redundancy, replication, and failure-handling protocols.",
"Partitioning": "The division of a dataset or workload across multiple nodes, also known as sharding, to enable horizontal scalability. Partitioning distributes storage and processing load but introduces complexity in cross-partition operations.",
"Node": "An individual computing entity, such as a server or process, that participates as a member of a distributed system. Nodes communicate via message passing to collectively perform system functions.",
"Data Distribution": "The strategy and arrangement by which data is spread across multiple nodes in a distributed system. It encompasses techniques like partitioning and replication to balance load, locality, and reliability.",
"Consistency Model": "A formal contract specifying the guarantees a distributed system provides regarding the visibility and ordering of updates to shared data. Different models represent different trade-offs between correctness, performance, and availability.",
"Safety": "A property ensuring that nothing bad happens in a system, such as never returning incorrect or inconsistent results. In distributed systems, safety guarantees often constrain how aggressively performance optimizations can be applied.",
"Performance": "A measure of how efficiently a system executes operations, typically in terms of throughput, latency, and resource utilization. In distributed systems, performance is often traded against consistency and fault tolerance.",
"Strong Consistency": "A consistency model in which all nodes observe operations in the same order and updates become immediately visible to all subsequent reads. It provides intuitive semantics at the cost of higher latency and reduced availability.",
"Eventual Consistency": "A consistency model that guarantees all replicas will converge to the same state given sufficient time without new updates, but permits temporary inconsistencies. It favors availability and performance over immediate correctness.",
"Update Visibility": "The point in time at which a write or modification becomes observable to readers across the distributed system. Different consistency models offer different guarantees about when and how updates become visible.",
"Temporary Divergence": "A condition in which replicas of the same data hold differing values for a limited period before reconciling. It is a characteristic of eventually consistent systems and reflects the trade-off between availability and immediate consistency."
}
